slides.title: First, a confession
slides.caption: Unrelated. A good boy in a DEV DOG hoodie who commits with "woof". That is the whole joke. Moving on.

box.content:
I have deployed code on a Friday afternoon. I have also spent that weekend undoing it while a client called every two hours.

I am not here to sell you a future where software writes itself. I am here because the tools got genuinely useful, and nobody sat me down and explained how to actually work with them. So here is that class, condensed.

The goal is not to type less. The goal is to spend your thinking on the parts that need a human.

slides.title: The bug that taught me the most
slides.caption: The illustrator guessed Day 14. My actual log said sixteen.

box.content:
A self-checkout kiosk kept marking books as "not returned", only after 6 PM. Two weeks of logs. The reader was fine. The database was fine.

It was the tag UID. One vendor sent it most-significant byte first, the other least-significant. After 6 PM staff switched handhelds. The bytes were being compared in opposite order.

The fix was four lines. Finding it was fourteen days. That ratio never really changes — and it is exactly the part AI is worst at.

slides.title: Chapter 2 — From autocomplete to whatever this is
slides.subtitle: A short, opinionated history

slides.title: A very short history

list.text: Autocomplete era: it finished your line. Sometimes correctly.
Chat era (2022): you asked, it answered, you copied and pasted and prayed.
Editor copilots: it moved into the IDE and could see your open file.
Agent era (now): it reads the repo, runs the tests, reads the errors, and tries again.

slides.title: A chatbot vs an agent
leftPoints: You copy, paste, wire it up, and verify
Great for learning and getting unstuck
One turn at a time, you drive every step
rightPoints: Reads files, runs commands, edits code directly
Plans, acts, checks the result, corrects itself
Can read docs and confirm its own work
Chases a goal across many steps

note.text: Claude Code, Antigravity, and Codex are all in the right-hand column. That is the shift.

slides.title: The colleague who never sleeps and never brings snacks
slides.imageAlt: A frazzled four-armed robot coding at 2:47 AM surrounded by coffee cups
slides.caption: 2:47 AM. Fourth coffee. "Project: almost done." It is not almost done.
slides.content:
The word that matters is agency

A chatbot can explain a bug to you. An agent can open the file, reproduce the bug, patch it, run the suite, and hand you a diff. Same underlying model. Completely different thing to work with.

slides.title: Hot take
slides.caption: "Sleep is optional." "Deploy on Friday?" This wall is the argument for AI, not against it.

box.content:
Most "AI will replace developers" posts are written by people who have never been paged at 3 AM to fix a data migration.

The job was never typing. It is deciding what to build, and being the person who understands the system when it breaks. AI moves the typing. It does not move the responsibility.

slides.question: What is the single biggest difference between a conversational AI and an agentic one?
options: The agent uses a larger model
The agent can take actions in your environment, not just answer
There is no real difference, it is marketing
slides.explanation: Agency (reading, acting, and checking inside your actual environment) is what separates a chat window from a coding agent.

slides.title: The skill that matters now
slides.caption: "Algorithms and Suffering" is not a real book. It should be. Fundamentals still win.

list.text: Prompting — giving enough context and clear constraints.
Verifying — reading output like you would review a stranger's PR.
Security sense — not pasting secrets, not trusting generated auth code blindly.

slides.title: Chapter 3 — Using it without making a mess
slides.subtitle: Where it helps, where it lies, and how to ask

slides.title: Old loop vs new loop
slides.caption: "PROJECT CHAOS (DOOMED)." This is the old loop, unfiltered.

list.text: Old: plan, write, test, review, deploy — every step by hand.
New: same steps, but an agent drafts, explains, and tests alongside you, while you decide what "correct" means.

slides.title: Where it pulls its weight vs where it lies
leftPoints: Explaining a codebase you were just handed
First-draft tests for code that already works
Debugging with a real stack trace in hand
rightPoints: Architecture and trade-offs — it will pick one and defend it
Security review — it misses the subtle holes, cheerfully
Domain judgement — it does not know your users or your rules
"Is this actually correct" — only you and the tests can answer that

note.text: It is never unsure. That is the dangerous part.

slides.title: A real conversation, lightly edited

box.content:
Me: add pagination to the users endpoint

Done. Added limit and offset params, a total count, and updated the docs.

Me: that file you edited is not the users endpoint

You are absolutely right, and I apologise for the confusion. Correcting it now.

Me: also this is FastAPI, not Flask

Of course. My mistake. Here is the version using FastAPI Query parameters.

Me: ok that one actually works

Glad I could help. Would you like me to add tests?

Me: ...yes

note.text: This is the normal experience. It is still faster than doing it alone. You just have to stay in the room.

slides.title: Bad prompt / good prompt

box.title: Same request, very different afternoon
box.code:
// Vague - invites guessing
"fix my code"

// Specific - grounded in reality
"In src/api/users.py, GET /users/{id} returns 500
when id is not numeric. Traceback below. Add
validation that returns 400 with a clear message,
matching validate_order_id() in src/api/orders.py.
<paste traceback>"

slides.title: Before you let it near main

list.text: Read every line. Do not merge what you have not read.
Actually run it. Do not just nod at it.
Grep for keys, tokens, and hardcoded credentials.
Be able to explain it — in review, in a viva, in an interview.

note.text: Rule of thumb: if you would be embarrassed to have written it, do not ship it under your name.

slides.title: The human stays in the loop
slides.imageAlt: A team meeting where the whiteboard reads AI DO NOT TOUCH MAIN BRANCH and a cheerful robot says I CAN DO THAT
slides.caption: The whiteboard says do not touch main. The robot says "I can do that." Your job is to stay between them.
slides.content:
Every workflow here has a human checkpoint

That is not overcaution. It is the line between using AI as a tool and quietly outsourcing your judgement to it.

slides.title: Chapter 4 — The actual tools
slides.subtitle: What each one is, and when to reach for it

slides.title: What we will actually look at

list.text: ESP-IDF — the framework ESP32 firmware is built in.
GitHub — repos, CI/CD, and where most AI tools plug in.
Google Antigravity — Google DeepMind's agentic IDE.
OpenAI Codex — OpenAI's cloud and CLI coding agent.
Claude Code — Anthropic's terminal-first agent.

slides.title: ESP-IDF — where the firmware lives
slides.imageAlt: Isometric cartoon of a circuit board drawn as a small town called Microville
slides.caption: Welcome to Microville, population 1024. Every IoT project starts in a town like this.
slides.content:
Espressif's official SDK for ESP32-class chips

  • Built on FreeRTOS — real multitasking on a microcontroller.
  • idf.py to build and flash, menuconfig for build options.
  • JTAG and OpenOCD for real debugging, not just serial-print archaeology.

slides.title: GitHub — the boring backbone that runs everything

list.text: Repos and pull requests — where review actually happens.
Actions — the pipeline that deploys Circuit Digest Cloud.
Copilot — inline, autocomplete-style suggestions.

slides.title: Codex & Antigravity, in 60 seconds

list.title: OpenAI Codex
list.text: Cloud + CLI agent. Runs in a sandbox and hands work back as a reviewable pull request. Best on well-scoped jobs.

list.title: Google Antigravity
list.text: Agentic IDE with browser sub-agents that verify UI changes visually, and deep whole-codebase context.

slides.title: Claude Code

list.text: Reads and edits files, and runs your commands directly.
MCP lets it connect to external tools and data sources.
Plan mode proposes a plan for you to approve before it touches anything.

note.text: This deck was assembled with Claude Code, in this project's own repo.

slides.title: Free tools, hackathons, and where to compete

box.title: The shortcuts nobody tells you about

list.text: GitHub Student Developer Pack — free Copilot, Codespaces, Azure credit, and every JetBrains IDE. Verify once at education.github.com.
Open source — search "good first issue" on GitHub, or wait for Hacktoberfest every October.
Hackathons — MLH and Devfolio for the weekend circuit, Smart India Hackathon for the real thing.
Competitions — Google Summer of Code if you want to get paid for open source, Kaggle if data is your thing.

note.text: Pick one of these to actually do this month. Bookmarking is not participation.

slides.title: If you remember four things
slides.caption: Do these four and the line goes up. Results may vary. Line not to scale.

list.text: Circuit Digest turns electronics knowledge into tutorials and real infrastructure.
AI moved from answering to acting. That is the whole story of the last two years.
Keep a human checkpoint before and after the agent acts.
ESP-IDF, GitHub, Antigravity, Codex, Claude Code — each solves a different slice.
